did_you_know.text: The name Cain sounds like the Hebrew word qaniti, “I have acquired,” creating a wordplay between the child’s name and Eve’s words.
The name Abel means “breath” or “vapor.” The same Hebrew root appears in Ecclesiastes for something fleeting and unstable.
Sin is pictured as a dangerous animal crouching at the door and waiting for an opportunity. Yet the verse stresses that a person can master it.
The question “Am I my brother’s keeper?” became a well-known expression in many languages and is still used when discussing our responsibility toward others.
The Bible never explains what Cain’s mark was. It only emphasizes that its purpose was to protect him from revenge.
The land of Nod is not identified with a known location. Its name is related to the Hebrew root meaning “to wander,” fitting Cain’s punishment.
This is the Bible’s first mention of a man taking two wives. The text reports it but does not explicitly say that it is right or desirable.
The word “father” here can mean not only a family parent but also a founder or pioneer in a field. Early culture is thus represented through herders, musicians, and craftspeople.
The phrase “to call on the name of the Lord” is often understood as the beginning of public prayer or worship. Scholars also note that the Hebrew may mean proclaiming or invoking God’s name.
